Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2 # Chapter 2 Silver ## Renewed economic slowdown has taken its toll on silver Global economic growth has continued to slow during the last three months and this has had further repercussions for silver. We already knew that fabrication demand was beginning to be curtailed in the second half of last year and evidence is pointing to a further weakening since then. Silver’s industrial metal credentials are therefore in control, just as they were during the Global Financial Crisis in 2008-09. Its average price in the final week of March was in excess of $32/oz, and it had fallen to trade at around $27/oz in late June. It has therefore lost about 15% of its US dollar value. Moreover, it’s 45% below its peak of $48.70/oz in April 2011. The latest falls in industrial metal prices have been prompted by concerns about China as much as the Eurozone. The currencies of each of these have weakened during the last three months. However, most of the economic malaise has stemmed from the Eurozone, and the euro Silver is still relatively strong in comparison with other metals

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2 Silver 86 has fallen by 5% against the US dollar during this period. The strengthening of the US dollar has undoubtedly contributed to the fall in silver’s price, but silver’s weakening consumption prospects have arguably played the greatest role. The gold:silver price ratio h

as increased from 51-52 in late March to 58-59 in late June.  Gold has therefore lost only 6% of its value during this period while euro-denominated quotations have slipped by no more than 1%. 

Investors’ interest in ETFs has remained relatively muted.  Holdings are no longer falling as they did after peaking in March 2011 through to the end of 2011.  They fell by 829 tonnes during that period but have since recovered by only 469 tonnes.  Much of this subsequent rise could have been missed by some because it because 70% of it was attributable to the lesser known Sprott Trust.  However, total reported stocks have continued to increase beyond their peak.  Comex inventories have increased by almost 1,500 tonnes from their trough.  Although total stocks slipped by 370 tonnes in 2011, they have since jumped by about 1,370 tonnes. 

## Consumption prospects worsen alongside stalling economy 

The current economic slowdown got underway in earnest in the third quarter of 2011 when it became clear that activity in China, as well as in Europe, had eased.  This made 2011 a year of two halves, with second-half growth being unable to sustain increasing levels of fabrication. Indeed, our tabulations now have offtake slipping by a modest 320 tonnes (or 1-1.5%) to 26,620 tonnes.  This measure includes silver used in coins and medals.  If this is excluded, residual consumption fell by 910 tonnes (or 3.5-4%) to 22,940 tonnes. 

Europe has been at the heart of this slowdown.  Estimates of industrial production in this region in 2008-11 have been cut with the cumulative impact reducing absolute activity in 2011 by 0.3%.  Meanwhile, our latest forecast for 2013 is 0.8% lower than what our tabulations were based on in March.  Our figures for industrial demand have therefore been cut throughout our forecast and, from a lower base in 2011, we now have total fabrication in 2016 of 28,550 tonnes which is 900 tonnes less than we were previously quoting.  Although the increase in 2011-16 is just 1,930 tonnes, the rise is twice as large when silver’s use in coins and medals is excluded. 

We believe that demand stemming from coinage is now beyond its peak but assume that volumes will largely be maintained in the short term as it continues to be an attractive product in light of the nervousness surrounding the global economy.  In turn, we believe that an eventual economic recovery will be the catalyst for a sharp drop in offtake in this market.  Silver’s use in photography will also decline, although we continue to believe that this will not be rapid.  On the one hand, the digital photography market is now mature and so there is not much scope for demand for consumer film to fall further.  Meanwhile, digital technology is unlikely to erode silver’s use in radiography very quickly in light of conservative public spending plans. 

## Today’s mines are still due to supply 27,000 tonnes in 2016 

We have cut out estimate of global mine output in 2011 by 69 tonnes to 24,391 tonne

s. This was largely attributable to obtaining Wolverine’s production numbers and this mine contributed 127 tonnes less to Canadian supply than we were previously estimating. Hidden Valley and Kazakhyms also produced less than we were expecting. In contrast we have raised our estimate of Mexican output. Our interpretation of revisions to the official numbers has led us to raise our figure by 172 tonnes. Growth in Zacatecas is largely attributable to the new Saucito mine. The global total in 2011 was up by just 1.4%, which is much slower than the average annual rate of 4% in 2009-10. This slowdown is the result of South American supplies falling from their peak. Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2 Silver 88 Although we still have global mine supply totalling 27,000 tonnes in 2016, the cumulative total in 2012-16 has been cut by 1,950 tonnes. This revision has largely materialised in 2012-14 as a result of more conservative projections for Marlin and a number of mines in Australia, and due to Kagara’s suspension of operations in response to low Australian dollar-denominated zinc prices. With zinc and lead prices continuing to slip, we are assuming that there is scope for further curtailments in by-product silver supply. Moreover, project financing remains difficult for a number of potential producers and the recent fall in silver’s price will make it difficult for even potential main-producer miners to raise sufficient finance. Our tabulations reflect this too. ## The future surplus will be greater than previously forecast We now estimate that a surplus of almost 6,500 tonnes was generated in 2011 and this is roughly 2,800 tonnes greater than we quoted last time. This is the result of fabrication demand slowing even more sharply than we previously stated and, while mine output may have fallen slightly short of what we last said, the spike in silver’s price encouraged a surge in supply from recycled scrap. Stocks rose to the equivalent of 1.8 years of consumption at the end of 2011, up from 1.5 year at the end of 2010, and this is the highest this measure has been since 1995. With it starting from a weaker base in 2011 and following a lower path from there, reduced fabrication demand will contribute an extra 6,275 tonnes to the cumulative surplus in 2012-16. Ho
